extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys and applicants (AMS patent offices / PCT practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing inventive step (non-obviousness) and industrial applicability during patent examination, including tests (problem-solution, Windsurfing/Pozzoli), definition and scope of the Person Skilled in the Art, combining prior art, secondary considerations, claim dependency, and rules on amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step approach for testing inventive step: (i) determining the closest prior art; (ii) establishing the objective technical problem to be solved; and (iii) considering whether or not the claimed invention, starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem, would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the third stage the examiner asks whether any teaching in the prior art as a whole would (not simply could, but would) have prompted the PSIA, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify or adapt the closest prior art so as to arrive at subject-matter within the terms of the claims and achieve the invention. (See EPO Guidelines Part G, Ch VII para 5.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing/Pozzoli test
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step test for obviousness: (i) identify the claimed inventive concept; (ii) assume the mantle of the PSIA on the relevant date and impute common general knowledge; (iii) identify differences between the prior art and the alleged invention; (iv) decide, without knowledge of the alleged invention, whether these differences would have been obvious to the PSIA or require invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Windsurfing/Pozzoli test does not require identifying the 'closest prior art' (unlike the problem-solution approach); it requires identifying the most relevant 'prior art'. Pozzoli restatement: (1)(a) identify the notional PSIA (b) identify relevant common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept or construe the claim; (3) identify differences between prior art and inventive concept/claim; (4) viewed without knowledge of the invention, would the differences be obvious to the PSIA?

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical person with common general knowledge in the art and the ability to use ordinary technical means for R&D, with average or ordinary skills; not the inventor; able to exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials and optimizing ranges but without inventive capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSIA's exact level of knowledge and skill is case-specific. Standard excludes persons of extraordinary skill. PSIA may be an individual or, in some advanced/complex fields, a group (e.g., research or production team). The core question is whether the PSIA would arrive at the alleged invention without exercising inventive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of knowledge of the PSIA
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSIA is presumed to have common general knowledge and: (I) access to all publicly available prior art; (II) ability to comprehend all technical matters in the relevant art; (III) capability to apply conventional experimental methods available before the date but no capacity for creativity; (IV) awareness of what was common general and field-specific knowledge at the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common general knowledge can be evidenced by textbooks, handbooks, monographs, encyclopedias and reference books. Certain self-evident scientific features may be assumed within the PSIA's intellectual arsenal. If the technical problem prompts searching another field, the skilled person in that field may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of combining prior art (mosaicing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two or more prior art references is permissible only where such combination would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners usually consider: (i) whether the nature and content of the prior arts make it likely the PSIA would combine them; (ii) whether the prior arts come from similar or neighbouring technical fields, or are reasonably pertinent to the problem. A combination is allowable only where a PSIA would be motivated with reasonable likelihood to combine, substitute or modify prior art teachings. Motivation need not be the same as the applicant’s; combining parts of the same document requires a reasonable basis to associate them. Textbooks/standards are generally obvious to combine with other documents; documents with clear references to each other likewise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection inventions (selected sub-sets or sub-ranges) differ from the closest prior art and may involve an inventive step if the selection is connected to a particular technical effect and no indications exist that would lead the PSIA to the selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical effect occurring within the selected range may be the same effect as in the broader known range but to an unexpected degree. Consider whether the PSIA would have made the selection or chosen an overlapping range in expectation of improvement; if negative, inventive step accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (indications of inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be taken into account as persuasive pointers towards non-obviousness: (i) whether the invention fulfils a long-felt need; (ii) whether it overcomes a scientific prejudice; (iii) whether others previously attempted but failed to achieve it; (iv) whether it involves an unexpected result; (v) whether it has particular commercial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are supplementary to the formal tests and may be technical or commercial in nature; further national practices vary among AMS. See detailed technical and commercial factors below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical secondary factors (guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical indicators include overcoming a scientific prejudice, teaching away, unexpected technical advance, and evidence of long-felt need or prior failed attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overcoming a scientific prejudice: examiners should hesitate to find lack of inventive step where the invention solves a long-standing technical problem or overcomes prejudice. Teaching away: if prior art would have led the PSIA away from the invention, that supports inventive step. Unexpected technical progress: must derive from the claimed subject-matter (characterising features) and be described precisely — vague assertions are insufficient. Foreseeable disadvantageous modification or arbitrary non-functional changes normally do not confer inventive step unless accompanied by unexpected advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial secondary factors (guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial or economic success may indicate inventive step but is not sufficient alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is relevant only if examiner is satisfied the success derives from technical features of the claimed invention (not from marketing, selling techniques or advertising) and is commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. Coupled evidence of long-felt need strengthens the pointer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the inventor-disclosed problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure should allow the technical problem(s) and the solution to be appreciated; this relevance is considered when assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only details necessary for elucidating the invention should be included; when in doubt examiners should not require excision. It is not necessary to present the invention explicitly in problem-and-solution form. See PCT ISPE GL Ch 4 para 4.07 re: disclosure of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the technical problem in selecting the test
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance attached to the technical problem affects which inventive-step test is used: high importance -> problem-solution approach; medium importance -> Windsurfing/Pozzoli test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem-solution approach used in Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam; Windsurfing test used in Malaysia and Singapore. The choice reflects national practice and the role ascribed to the technical problem in assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and evidential requirement for advantageous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantageous effects can support inventive step only if they derive from the characterising features of the claim, not merely from description-only features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected effect must be described precisely; vague statements (e.g., 'unexpectedly good pharmaceutical properties') cannot support inventive step. The effect must be tied to claimed features in combination with known features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose advantageous effects in the application
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS require the description to specifically state advantageous effects of the claimed invention; others do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any advantageous effects the applicant considers relevant should be stated, but not in a way that disparages prior products or misleads (e.g., ambiguous presentation implying prior art solved less than was the case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of later-submitted data when assessing inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Later-submitted data will be considered by the examiner only if the submission is made in response to an office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The data must not go beyond the scope of the original application or provide a new teaching. Whether the response is admitted depends on the individual case; evidence must be supported by the original disclosure to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality and evidential standard for advantageous effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper or hypothetical examples of advantageous effects may be insufficient if contrary evidence exists; advantageous effects should be described via structural analysis, theoretical explanation or experiential data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should seek concrete analysis linking structural features of the invention to the claimed advantageous effect; unsupported or purely speculative assertions are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations indicating lack of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention results from a foreseeable disadvantageous modification of the closest prior art, which the skilled person could predict and assess, and no unexpected technical advantage is present, then the claimed invention does not involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar considerations apply where the invention is merely an arbitrary non-functional modification or an arbitrary choice from many possible solutions. See EPO Guidelines para 10.1 re: predictable disadvantage; non-functional modification; arbitrary choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims dependency and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims are regarded as limited by all features of the claims on which they depend; inventive-step assessment should reflect this dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an independent claim has a positive inventive-step finding, dependent claims should normally also be positive. If an independent claim lacks inventive step, the examiner must assess each dependent claim separately. PCT ISPE GL and EPO Guidelines provide examples and stress examiners should avoid trying to force-fit a case into examples that do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability requirement (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial applicability (susceptibility of industrial application) is a patentability requirement: an invention must be capable of being made or used in some kind of industry (broadly construed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Industry' should be understood in a broad sense (including agriculture, handicraft). Industrial applicability does not override exclusions on patentable subject-matter (e.g., surgical methods on the human body). Inoperative inventions (contrary to well-established laws of nature) lack industrial applicability and should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability test (three conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet industrial applicability a patent application must satisfy: (1) indicate the way the invention is capable of exploitation in industry (intended function/specific use); (2) disclose the invention in a sufficiently clear and complete manner for a PSIA to carry it out (possibly relying on public prior sources); (3) it must actually be possible for a PSIA to realize the indicated special purpose when carrying out any claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special purpose should be apparent from the claim or nature of the invention (e.g., a computer vs. a novel chemical compound which may need a specific use). Clear and complete disclosure may be satisfied by application together with public prior art; but if necessary manufacturing information is absent and not publicly available, the second requirement fails. Possibility of realising the special purpose is a technical verification — e.g., a 'perpetuum mobile' fails despite adequate disclosure if contrary to physical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date at which industrial applicability requirements must be met
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification of compliance with industrial applicability requirements is carried out as of the priority date of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information incorporated into the application after the priority date cannot be used to establish industrial applicability as of the priority date; such incorporation may be regarded as adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights against rejection for lack of industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner objects for lack of industrial applicability, the applicant should be allowed to respond and submit explanations, data or evidence to address examiner's objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission of the response depends on the case; usually submissions supported by the original disclosure may be considered. If the examiner upholds rejection, appeal to an upper administrative body or competent court is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rules on amendments (pre- and post-grant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments are normal; pre-grant amendments are allowed in all AMS, some allow post-grant amendment. Amendments must not add technical subject-matter beyond the original disclosure; correction of obvious mistakes is allowed both pre- and post-grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any pre- or post-grant amendment (other than rectification of obvious mistakes or furnishing missing parts) should be considered an amendment. Pre- and post-grant amendments must be formally and substantially allowable — they must not add subject-matter or introduce deficiencies such as lack of clarity or lack of unity. Practices on added matter are consistent across AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant amendment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main ways to file pre-grant amendments: (a) voluntary amendment before filing the search and examination request (subject to prescribed manner, documents and fees); (b) amending when responding to the examiner’s written opinion or objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant is not entitled to amend unless a request is made in the prescribed manner, within prescribed period, accompanied by prescribed documents and fees. Failure to comply may lead to refusal of the request. Pre-grant changes must be considered for search/examination unless filed after search and concern unsearched subject-matter (varies by jurisdiction).
